articles.title: Private Browser File Uploads: Object Storage Service and 3-Stage Throughput
articles.excerpt: Short answer: for a marketplace accepting private browser uploads, the least complex design is a direct-to-object-storage upload followed by backend processing and an expiring download URL. Presigning…
articles.body: Short answer: for a marketplace accepting private browser uploads, the least complex design is a direct-to-object-storage upload followed by backend processing and an expiring download URL. Presigning itself is not the cost decision. Storage, API calls, and the throughput behavior of large objects are. My default shortlist is Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, and Google Cloud Storage, with Infrai as a reasonable fourth option when the processing call and worker queue should share the storage credential. The winner depends on the upload size, region, concurrency, and the controls the marketplace cannot compromise. Start small. Which object storage service should handle browser file uploads? The browser asks the backend for a short-lived signed upload URL.

articles.excerpt: If you want to use Next.js as the frontend for a headless CMS, this covers where to host it and what each option costs you in money and DevOps effort. On paper, Next.js runs anywhere Node.js runs, esp…
articles.body: If you want to use Next.js as the frontend for a headless CMS, this covers where to host it and what each option costs you in money and DevOps effort. On paper, Next.js runs anywhere Node.js runs, especially with the official Deployment Adapters API introduced in Next.js 16.2. In production it's a different story. A headless CMS frontend depends on multi-layered caching, webhook-driven revalidation, image optimization and isolated preview environments, and the caching features (ISR, tag-based revalidation, App Router data caches and next/image ) behave very differently depending on where you host.

articles.excerpt: If you want to pick a frontend framework for a headless CMS website, this covers the SPA and MPA options I'd consider and when each one fits. Download the one-page framework comparison (PDF) On a trad…
articles.body: If you want to pick a frontend framework for a headless CMS website, this covers the SPA and MPA options I'd consider and when each one fits. Download the one-page framework comparison (PDF) On a traditional CMS like standard WordPress or Drupal, the frontend is mostly a skin. The CMS owns URL routing, database queries, HTML assembly and page delivery out of the box, and developers style theme templates and add some JavaScript on top. When you go headless, the backend steps back and becomes a content repository and an API. The frontend takes over everything the public sees: URL routing and slug resolution: mapping thousands of editorial paths, nested categories and localized URLs to the right content.

articles.title: Test 4.20 MHz Ultrasonic Protein Fibril Alignment in 48 Hours for $385 — Zero Microbes Required (Open-Source MRL-2 Bench Protocol)

articles.body: Most discussions around synthetic biology or alternative protein biomanufacturing assume you need a sterile BSL-1 fermenter, a gas-diffusion electrolyzer, and weeks of strain engineering before you can test whether a hardware architecture actually works. That assumption hides the single highest-risk physics stop-gate in cell-free acoustic protein structuring: Can a 4.20 MHz ultrasonic standing-wave cavity align a dense 180 g/L food-grade plant/microbial protein suspension into anisotropic meat-like fibrils ( 178 µm nodal pitch) without locally cooking the gel via viscous acoustic attenuation before enzymatic cross-linking locks in? You don't need a single living microbe, a bioreactor, or a microbiology permit to test and falsify that physics question.

articles.body: Continue's Docs Crawler Turned a Documentation URL Into an SSRF Path Developer tools that index documentation need to fetch remote pages. That convenience creates a server-side request boundary. Continue versions 2.0.0 and 2.1.0 contain a server-side request forgery flaw in the documentation crawler, tracked as CVE-2026-133695. The affected code is DocsCrawler in core/indexing/docs/crawlers/DocsCrawler.ts . The public description says a URL processed by the crawler can cause requests to destinations the user did not intend. The CVSS v3 score is 5.0, while the CVSS v4 score is 2.3 because the scoring model treats attack requirements and user interaction differently.

Per his post and GitHub write-up, covered by Tom's Hardware on November 20, 2026, the whole build cost $9,450 . The machine now runs DeepSeek V4.1 Flash with all 15,360 routed experts resident in memory at 4-bit NVFP4 , and his repo notes none of them were compressed further. Twelve cards lift total HBM2 memory to 384 GiB , so the full expert set fits without further shrinking.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 21, 1676: Danish astronomer discovers speed of light — by accident — while observing Jupiter's moon Io
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of lightwhile observing Jupiter and its moon volcanic moon Io. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of light . Before Rømer figured it out, scientists thought that light travels instantaneously, or infinitely fast. Rømer disproved this almost by accident when he was studying Jupiter's moon Io . He was trying to figure out how long it takes Io to orbit Jupiter in hopes of using it as a cosmic clock. He watched Io disappear behind Jupiter and reappear on the other side. He did this over and over every 42 hours for years. To his surprise, the timing of the eclipses was not consistent. When Earth was closest to Jupiter, the eclipses happened 11 minutes early. Likewise, when the two planets were farthest away, the eclipses were 11 minutes behind schedule.

articles.body: The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again. That vehicle, known as Ship 42, launched Nov. 13 on Starship 's 15th test flight. A day later, it returned from orbit, nestling softly into the "chopstick" arms of its launch tower at SpaceX 's Starbase site in South Texas. Ship 42 made it through Flight 15 in good condition, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk , who said it "could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment." But that's not going to happen. "In this case, because it's kind of an historic ship, we're going to, I think, not take any chances with the ship and just kind of leave it for public display, because what it's done is historic," Musk said on Wednesday (Nov. 18) during a discussion at the TomorrowX Summit .

articles.title: European-Japanese BepiColombo probe arrives in orbit around Mercury today
articles.excerpt: The BepiColombo spacecraft will finally arrive in orbit around Mercury today (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet.
articles.body: Mercury is about to receive a robotic visitor from Earth. The BepiColombo mission — a joint effort of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency ( JAXA ) — will arrive in orbit around Mercury today (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet. The big moment will come after an orbit-insertion burn, which is scheduled to begin today at 1:24 p.m. EST (1824 GMT) and last for 37 minutes. BepiColombo consists of two main spacecraft: ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO), also known as Mio.

articles.excerpt: SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force tonight (Nov. 20), sending a mystery payload to orbit from California's central coast.
articles.body: SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force tonight (Nov. 20), sending a mystery payload to orbit from California's central coast. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:20 p.m. EST (8:20 p.m. local California time; 0420 GMT on Nov. 21), on a Space Force mission called USSF-317. The Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth about 8.5 minutes later, touching down in the Pacific Ocean atop the SpaceX drone ship "Of Course I Still Love You." It was the 11th launch and landing for this booster, which is designated B1100. A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launches the USSF-317 mission for the U.S. Space Force from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California on Nov. 20, 2026.
